warmup.q: settle(batch) is annotated @Retry(attempts = 3) and calls this.audit(batch), which is also @Retry(attempts = 3) and always throws a retryable exception. The bean is intercepted by a subclass proxy, so self-calls are intercepted. How many times does audit's body run before settle gives up?
warmup.why: Each attempt of settle calls audit through the subclass, and audit's own retry runs its body three times before it throws. settle's retry then catches that and tries again, three times in all: 3 x 3 = 9. Nested retries multiply. With a forwarding proxy the inner call would skip interception and run once per settle attempt, 3 in all.

sections.h: An interceptor runs around a call, and proceed() is the call
sections.html:
Here is what timing and retries look like when every method does them itself:

Java
public String authorize(String pan, long amountMinor) {
    long t0 = System.nanoTime();
    try {
        for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
            try { return http.authorize(pan, amountMinor); }
            catch (IssuerUnavailableException e) { if (attempt == 3) throw e; }
        }
    } finally {
        metrics.record("authorize", System.nanoTime() - t0);
    }
}
Kotlin
fun authorize(pan: String, amountMinor: Long): String {
    val t0 = System.nanoTime()
    try {
        var attempt = 1
        while (true) {
            try { return http.authorize(pan, amountMinor) }
            catch (e: IssuerUnavailableException) { if (attempt++ == 3) throw e }
        }
    } finally {
        metrics.record("authorize", System.nanoTime() - t0)
    }
}

Two lines of business logic, twelve lines of plumbing, copied into capture, refund and void. Decorator and Proxy moved the plumbing into a class that wraps the client, but you still write one decorator per interface.

An interceptor is the plumbing written once, for any method. It receives an Invocation: the method's name, its arguments, and proceed(), which means "carry on with the call". Here is the lab's timer:

Java
public Object intercept(Invocation inv) {
    long start = clock.getAsLong();
    boolean failed = true;
    try {
        Object result = inv.proceed();
        failed = false;
        return result;
    } finally {
        log.record(inv.getName(), clock.getAsLong() - start, failed);
    }
}
Kotlin
override fun intercept(inv: Invocation): Any? {
    val start = clock.asLong
    var failed = true
    try {
        return inv.proceed().also { failed = false }
    } finally {
        log.record(inv.name, clock.asLong - start, failed)
    }
}

Several interceptors form a chain. proceed() runs the next one, and after the last one it runs the real method. A retry interceptor is a loop that calls proceed() again after a listed failure. CDI's InvocationContext.proceed() and Spring's MethodInvocation.proceed() have exactly this shape.

The order of the chain changes what you measure. With @Timed outside @Retry, the timer sees one call that took as long as all the attempts together. With @Timed inside, it records every attempt separately. The lab puts @Timed first, because the caller waited for all of it. The annotations themselves only mark methods: they need @Retention(RUNTIME) so the container can read them with getAnnotation, as @Component did in lesson 1.

try.title: Swap the order of two interceptors
steps: Read ChainDemo (or the Kotlin twin). The "issuer" fails twice and then answers. A third interceptor prints each time the chain reaches it.
Predict for each order: how many -> lines, and how many entries in the log?
Run it. Then change RetryInterceptor(3, ...) to RetryInterceptor(2, ...) and predict what the first order prints.

code.title: ChainDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo; import workbench.container.l02.CallLog; import workbench.container.l02.Interceptor; import workbench.container.l02.Invocation; import workbench.container.l02.RetryInterceptor; import workbench.container.l02.TimedInterceptor; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import java.util.function.LongSupplier; /** One issuer call that fails twice, sent through the same two interceptors in both orders. */ public class ChainDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { AtomicLong ticks = new AtomicLong(); LongSupplier clock = () -> ticks.addAndGet(10_000_000); // a fake clock: 10 ms per read Interceptor shout = inv -> { // a third interceptor, to watch proceed() System.out.println(" -> " + inv.getName()); try { return inv.proceed(); } finally { System.out.println(" <- " + inv.getName()); } }; for (String order : List.of("timed, retry", "retry, timed")) { CallLog log = new CallLog(); Interceptor timed = new TimedInterceptor(log, clock); Interceptor retry = new RetryInterceptor(3, List.of(IllegalStateException.class)); List<Interceptor> chain = order.startsWith("timed") ? List.of(timed, retry, shout) : List.of(retry, timed, shout); AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger(); System.out.println(order + ":"); Object result = new Invocation("Issuer.authorize", new Object[] {"4111111111111111"}, chain, () -> { if (calls.incrementAndGet() < 3) throw new IllegalStateException("issuer timed out"); // fails twice return "auth-1111"; }).proceed(); System.out.println(" result " + result + " after " + calls.get() + " calls, log " + log.calls()); } } }

alt.title: ChainDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo import workbench.container.l02.CallLog import workbench.container.l02.Interceptor import workbench.container.l02.Invocation import workbench.container.l02.RetryInterceptor import workbench.container.l02.TimedInterceptor import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong import java.util.function.LongSupplier // One issuer call that fails twice, sent through the same two interceptors in both orders. fun main() { val ticks = AtomicLong() val clock = LongSupplier { ticks.addAndGet(10_000_000) } // a fake clock: 10 ms per read val shout = Interceptor { inv -> // a third interceptor, to watch proceed() println(" -> ${inv.name}") try { inv.proceed() } finally { println(" <- ${inv.name}") } } for (order in listOf("timed, retry", "retry, timed")) { val log = CallLog() val timed = TimedInterceptor(log, clock) val retry = RetryInterceptor(3, listOf(IllegalStateException::class.java)) val chain = if (order.startsWith("timed")) listOf(timed, retry, shout) else listOf(retry, timed, shout) var calls = 0 println("$order:") val result = Invocation("Issuer.authorize", arrayOf("4111111111111111"), chain) { if (++calls < 3) throw IllegalStateException("issuer timed out") // fails twice "auth-1111" }.proceed() println(" result $result after $calls calls, log ${log.calls()}") } }

try.expect: Both orders print three ->/<- pairs, because the retry calls proceed() three times. With timed outside, the log has one entry, failed=false, 10 ms on the fake clock. With retry outside, it has three: two failed=true, one failed=false. With two attempts the call throws IllegalStateException: issuer timed out after two pairs, and the one log entry is recorded with failed=true on the way out.

sections.h: A component with interfaces gets a JDK proxy, and the handler owes four answers
sections.html:
The container now decides, for each component, how its interceptors will run. If the component implements an interface, it gets a JDK proxy: Proxy.newProxyInstance generates a class that implements the interfaces and sends every call to an InvocationHandler, as Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy showed. The container creates the real object first, the target, and the proxy holds it. Spring Framework's documented rule is the same: "If the target object to be proxied implements at least one interface, a JDK dynamic proxy is used." (Spring Boot switches its default to subclasses, as Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors showed.)

That lesson's handler rules come back as the four cases you write in the lab, in this order:

  1. equals, hashCode and toString arrive with method.declaringClass == Object. Answer them on the proxy, by identity. A handler that forwards equals to the target makes proxy.equals(proxy) false, and listeners.remove(proxy) quietly fails.
  2. A default method goes to InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, args), so its body runs with this being the proxy and its inner calls come back through the handler.
  3. Every other method builds an Invocation with that method's chain and a target call, method.invoke(target, args).
  4. That target call catches InvocationTargetException and rethrows its cause, so the caller sees the issuer's own IssuerUnavailableException.

Two consequences follow from "the proxy implements the interfaces". First, the bean is not a FakeIssuer. get(CardIssuerClient.class) works, but get(FakeIssuer.class) can't return a $Proxy5, so the lab's container refuses with a message naming the interface to ask for. Second, the handler only ever sees the interface's Method, so the annotations must be on the interface. @Timed on the class's method would never be read; the container refuses that at start-up too, rather than skipping it.

Kotlin's final-by-default doesn't matter on this path. FakeIssuer in the tests is a plain, final Kotlin class, and that's fine: the JDK only needs the interface.

code.title: ProxyIdentityDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo; import workbench.container.l02.Container; import workbench.container.l02.ContainerException; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.CardIssuerClient; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.FlakyIssuer; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.IssuerScript; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; /** The container's JDK proxy next to one whose handler forwards every method, equals included. */ public class ProxyIdentityDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Container c = new Container(List.of(IssuerScript.class, FlakyIssuer.class)); CardIssuerClient issuer = c.get(CardIssuerClient.class); System.out.println("bean class: " + issuer.getClass().getName() + " implements " + Arrays.stream(issuer.getClass().getInterfaces()).map(Class::getSimpleName).toList()); report("container's handler", issuer); FlakyIssuer target = new FlakyIssuer(new IssuerScript()); InvocationHandler forwardAll = (proxy, method, a) -> method.invoke(target, a); // equals goes to the target too report("forward everything", (CardIssuerClient) Proxy.newProxyInstance( CardIssuerClient.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[] {CardIssuerClient.class}, forwardAll)); try { c.get(FlakyIssuer.class); } catch (ContainerException e) { System.out.println("get(FlakyIssuer.class): " + e.getMessage()); } } static void report(String name, CardIssuerClient p) { List<CardIssuerClient> listeners = new ArrayList<>(List.of(p)); System.out.printf("%-20s p.equals(p)=%s listeners.remove(p)=%s hashCode is identity=%s%n", name, p.equals(p), listeners.remove(p), p.hashCode() == System.identityHashCode(p)); } }

alt.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo import workbench.container.l02.Container import workbench.container.l02.ContainerException import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.CardIssuerClient import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.FlakyIssuer import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.IssuerScript import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler import java.lang.reflect.Proxy // The container's JDK proxy next to one whose handler forwards every method, equals included. fun main() { val c = Container(listOf(IssuerScript::class.java, FlakyIssuer::class.java)) val issuer = c.get(CardIssuerClient::class.java) println("bean class: ${issuer.javaClass.name} implements ${issuer.javaClass.interfaces.map { it.simpleName }}") report("container's handler", issuer) val target = FlakyIssuer(IssuerScript()) val forwardAll = InvocationHandler { _, method, a -> method.invoke(target, *(a ?: emptyArray())) } // equals too report("forward everything", Proxy.newProxyInstance( CardIssuerClient::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(CardIssuerClient::class.java), forwardAll) as CardIssuerClient) try { c.get(FlakyIssuer::class.java) } catch (e: ContainerException) { println("get(FlakyIssuer::class.java): ${e.message}") } } private fun report(name: String, p: CardIssuerClient) { val listeners = mutableListOf(p) println("%-20s p.equals(p)=%s listeners.remove(p)=%s hashCode is identity=%s".format( name, p.equals(p), listeners.remove(p), p.hashCode() == System.identityHashCode(p))) }

try.expect: The bean is jdk.proxy2.$Proxy5 (the number depends on how many proxies the JVM made before, annotation instances included) and implements [CardIssuerClient]. The container's handler gives true true true. Forwarding everything gives false false false: the target was asked whether it equals the proxy, and said no. The last line is the container refusing get(FlakyIssuer.class): FlakyIssuer is behind a JDK proxy that implements [CardIssuerClient]; ask for one of those, not for the class.

sections.h: A class without interfaces gets a Byte Buddy subclass, so final is fatal
sections.html:
SettlementService has no interface, so the container generates a subclass with Byte Buddy, the "proxy is the object" model from Generated proxies: Byte Buddy, Spring AOP and Quarkus interceptors. Byte Buddy's subclass(type) copies the superclass's public constructors, so the container calls SettlementService$ByteBuddy$...(SettlementLedger) with the dependencies it resolved, and the original class is never instantiated on its own. There is one object. Each intercepted method is an override whose @SuperCall callable runs super.settle(...) at the end of the chain. A retry simply calls that callable again.

Because the subclass is the bean, a self-call goes through it. settle calls this.audit(batch), this is the subclass, and audit's override runs its own chain. The figure shows both models side by side.

A subclass can only intercept what it can override, and Kotlin makes that a daily problem. A Kotlin class is final unless you write open, and so is every member. On a final class Byte Buddy fails loudly: Cannot subclass primitive, array or final types. On an open class with a plain fun, it succeeds, and the method is simply not overridden. @Timed sits on it and does nothing. That silent case is why the lab's container calls check(component) for every component when it starts, and refuses a final class or a final or private intercepted method with a message that says what to change.

There are three fixes. Write open on the class and on each intercepted method. Or let the all-open compiler plugin do it for classes that carry an annotation you choose; this lab's build opens classes marked @OpenForProxies:

// container/build.gradle.kts
plugins { kotlin("plugin.allopen") }
allOpen { annotation("workbench.container.l02.demo.OpenForProxies") }

kotlin-spring is the same plugin, preset to open @Component and its friends. The third fix is an interface, which moves the component to the JDK-proxy path where finality doesn't matter. Quarkus goes a fourth way: with quarkus.arc.transform-unproxyable-classes, on by default, it rewrites final classes at build time so it can subclass them.

Each Byte Buddy class also gets its own class loader, a ByteArrayClassLoader, unless you choose another loading strategy. Lesson 3 counts what that costs.

sections.h: Retry the smallest call that is safe to repeat
sections.html:
A retry interceptor makes three promises. It only retries the exceptions the annotation lists: an IssuerUnavailableException is worth another try, a card number that fails the Luhn check is not. It counts attempts in total, so attempts = 3 means at most three calls. And when it gives up, the caller gets the original exception, not an UndeclaredThrowableException or an InvocationTargetException wrapped around it.

The hard part is choosing which call to repeat. authorizeAndCapture is a default method that calls authorize and then capture. If the handler forwards it to the target and retries it as a whole, a capture that times out repeats the authorization too: the issuer sees a second hold on the customer's card. With invokeDefault, the default body runs on the proxy, and each inner call carries its own @Retry. The capture is retried as a capture. That is the default-method rule from Dynamic proxies with java.lang.reflect.Proxy, and the lab tests it.

Even a single call is only safe to repeat when the other side can recognize the repeat. A timeout doesn't tell you the issuer didn't capture; it tells you that you don't know. So retry a capture only if it carries an idempotency key, the same one on every attempt, which the issuer uses to drop duplicates. The interceptor can't know that; the person who writes @Retry on the method has to.

Retries also nest. With a subclass proxy, a retried settle that calls a retried audit runs audit's body up to 3 x 3 = 9 times, as the warm-up asked. Put @Retry on the outermost call that is safe to repeat, or on the innermost one, and not on both.

try.title: Retry the capture, not the authorization
steps: Read RetryDemo (or the Kotlin twin). The issuer's first capture times out. The first half uses the container's proxy; the second uses a handler that retries every method as a whole.
Predict the list of calls the issuer sees in each half.

code.title: RetryDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo; import workbench.container.l02.Container; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.CardIssuerClient; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.FlakyIssuer; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.IssuerScript; import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.IssuerUnavailableException; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler; import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException; import java.lang.reflect.Proxy; import java.util.List; /** authorizeAndCapture, with one capture timing out: what does the issuer see? */ public class RetryDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { Container c = new Container(List.of(IssuerScript.class, FlakyIssuer.class)); IssuerScript script = c.get(IssuerScript.class); script.captureFailures.set(1); String result = c.get(CardIssuerClient.class).authorizeAndCapture("4111111111111111", 12_000); System.out.println("container's proxy: " + result + ", issuer saw " + script.seen); System.out.println(" timed calls: " + c.callLog().names()); IssuerScript naiveScript = new IssuerScript(); naiveScript.captureFailures.set(1); FlakyIssuer target = new FlakyIssuer(naiveScript); InvocationHandler retryEverything = (proxy, method, a) -> { // retries any method, default ones too for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) { try { return method.invoke(target, a); // the default body runs on the target } catch (InvocationTargetException e) { if (attempt == 3 || !(e.getCause() instanceof IssuerUnavailableException)) throw e.getCause(); } } }; CardIssuerClient naive = (CardIssuerClient) Proxy.newProxyInstance( CardIssuerClient.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[] {CardIssuerClient.class}, retryEverything); System.out.println("retry the shell: " + naive.authorizeAndCapture("4111111111111111", 12_000) + ", issuer saw " + naiveScript.seen); } }

alt.title: RetryDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.container.l02.demo import workbench.container.l02.Container import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.CardIssuerClient import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.FlakyIssuer import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.IssuerScript import workbench.container.l02.demo.app.IssuerUnavailableException import java.lang.reflect.InvocationHandler import java.lang.reflect.InvocationTargetException import java.lang.reflect.Method import java.lang.reflect.Proxy // authorizeAndCapture, with one capture timing out: what does the issuer see? fun main() { val c = Container(listOf(IssuerScript::class.java, FlakyIssuer::class.java)) val script = c.get(IssuerScript::class.java) script.captureFailures.set(1) val result = c.get(CardIssuerClient::class.java).authorizeAndCapture("4111111111111111", 12_000) println("container's proxy: $result, issuer saw ${script.seen}") println(" timed calls: ${c.callLog().names()}") val naiveScript = IssuerScript().apply { captureFailures.set(1) } val target = FlakyIssuer(naiveScript) val retryEverything = InvocationHandler { _, method, a -> callWithRetry(target, method, a) } // any method, defaults too val naive = Proxy.newProxyInstance(CardIssuerClient::class.java.classLoader, arrayOf(CardIssuerClient::class.java), retryEverything) as CardIssuerClient println("retry the shell: ${naive.authorizeAndCapture("4111111111111111", 12_000)}, issuer saw ${naiveScript.seen}") } private fun callWithRetry(target: Any, method: Method, a: Array<Any?>?, attempt: Int = 1): Any? = try { method.invoke(target, *(a ?: emptyArray())) // the default body runs on the target } catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { if (attempt == 3 || e.cause !is IssuerUnavailableException) throw e.cause!! callWithRetry(target, method, a, attempt + 1) }

try.expect: Both halves return cap-auth-1111. Through the container the issuer sees [authorize, capture (timed out), capture], and the timed calls are authorize and capture: the default method itself is not timed. The naive handler gives [authorize, capture (timed out), authorize, capture]: one customer, two authorizations.

analogy: A JDK proxy is a receptionist in front of a specialist's office. Every visitor goes through the receptionist, who logs the time and sends them back in if the specialist was busy, but when the specialist walks down the corridor to ask a colleague a question, no receptionist sees it. A Byte Buddy subclass is the specialist with a habit built in: they log their own time, even for questions they ask themselves. A final Kotlin class is a specialist who refuses to learn new habits, and the honest thing is to say so at hiring time. The analogy breaks at retries: a receptionist would notice a patient being sent in twice, while an interceptor repeats whatever you annotated, harmful or not.
world: This is the machinery under @Transactional, @Retry from SmallRye Fault Tolerance, Micrometer's @Timed and Spring's @Cacheable. In your Quarkus services ArC generates the subclass at build time and documents that self-calls are intercepted; in a Spring service the advice runs in a proxy in front of a separate target, and self-calls skip it. Before you put a retry on an issuer call, check that the request carries an idempotency key the issuer honours, and put the retry on the capture, not on a method that also authorizes. In Kotlin, make sure the class and the method are open: compile, run javap -p, and look for final.
mistake: The most common mistake is trusting that an annotation runs because it is on the method. Interception only happens when a call passes through generated code that can override or receive that method. A Kotlin method without open, a private method, a self-call on a forwarding proxy, an annotation placed on the class when the proxy only sees the interface: in each case the code compiles, the tests that call the class directly pass, and the timer or the retry never runs. People miss it because nothing fails. The fix is the lab's design: let the container check at start-up and refuse what it can't intercept, and test through the container with an assertion on the effect (a retry count, a log entry).

compare.title: An interceptable class in Java and in Kotlin

java.title: SettlementService.java
java.html: @Component public class SettlementService { // open unless you write final private final SettlementLedger ledger; public SettlementService(SettlementLedger ledger) { this.ledger = ledger; } @Timed public String settle(String batch) { // overridable audit(batch); // self-call: intercepted in a subclass ledger.post(batch); return "settled " + batch; } @Timed public void audit(String batch) { /* ... */ } public final String region() { return "EU"; } // final on purpose: not intercepted }

kotlin.title: SettlementService.kt
kotlin.html: @Component open class SettlementService(private val ledger: SettlementLedger) { // final without open @Timed open fun settle(batch: String): String { // final without open audit(batch) // self-call: intercepted in a subclass ledger.post(batch) return "settled $batch" } @Timed open fun audit(batch: String) { /* ... */ } fun region(): String = "EU" // final by default: not intercepted }

compare.note: The two classes compile to the same shape only after you add open in Kotlin. Java's default is overridable, so final is the exception you write; Kotlin's default is final, so open is. That single difference decides whether a subclass proxy can work, and on an open class with a plain fun it fails silently. The all-open plugin flips Kotlin's default for classes with an annotation you choose. Nothing differs for JDK proxies: both languages compile interfaces to ordinary JVM interfaces, and Kotlin interface functions with a body become JVM default methods that invokeDefault can run.

steps.say: Compliance wants every refund recorded with its arguments. Start with the marker. It needs RUNTIME retention and targets methods, like @Timed.
steps.code: @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Target(ElementType.METHOD) public @interface Audited { }

alt.html: @Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME) @Target(AnnotationTarget.FUNCTION) annotation class Audited

steps.say: Write the interceptor. It records the call before it proceeds, so an attempt that throws is in the audit trail too. It doesn't catch anything: failures are the retry's business, or the caller's.
steps.code: public final class AuditInterceptor implements Interceptor { private final List<String> trail; public AuditInterceptor(List<String> trail) { this.trail = trail; } @Override public Object intercept(Invocation inv) { trail.add(inv.getName() + Arrays.toString(inv.getArgs())); // 1. record first return inv.proceed(); // 2. then carry on } }

alt.html: class AuditInterceptor(private val trail: MutableList<String>) : Interceptor { override fun intercept(inv: Invocation): Any? { trail += inv.name + inv.args.contentToString() // 1. record first return inv.proceed() // 2. then carry on } }

steps.say: Decide where it goes in the chain. Outside @Retry, it records one entry per refund the caller asked for. Inside, it records every attempt. Compliance asked for every request sent to the issuer, so it goes inside: after the timer and the retry.
steps.code: List<Interceptor> chainFor(Method m) { List<Interceptor> chain = new ArrayList<>(); if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Timed.class)) chain.add(new TimedInterceptor(log, clock)); Retry r = m.getAnnotation(Retry.class); if (r != null) chain.add(new RetryInterceptor(r.attempts(), List.of(r.on()))); if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Audited.class)) chain.add(new AuditInterceptor(trail)); // 3. innermost return chain; }

alt.html: fun chainFor(m: Method): List<Interceptor> = buildList { if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Timed::class.java)) add(TimedInterceptor(log, clock)) m.getAnnotation(Retry::class.java)?.let { add(RetryInterceptor(it.attempts, it.on.map { k -> k.java })) } if (m.isAnnotationPresent(Audited::class.java)) add(AuditInterceptor(trail)) // 3. innermost }

steps.say: Teach the container that @Audited counts as intercepted, in isIntercepted, so check refuses a final audited method too. Then test through the container: a refund that times out once leaves two trail entries with the same idempotency key. If it leaves one, the interceptor is outside the retry; if it leaves none, the method was never overridden.

lab.title: Write the retry, the proxy handler and the start-up check
steps: Run the tests once. Eleven of twelve fail. The Java files in src/main/java/.../l02 are lesson 1's solution; Container now hands every component to Interception. The Kotlin files are yours. The fixtures are in src/test/kotlin/.../l02/Fixtures.kt: a scripted fake issuer and a few classes the container must refuse.
Write RetryInterceptor.intercept: a loop around inv.proceed() that rethrows on the last attempt or on an exception that isn't an instance of anything in retryOn.
Write InterceptingHandler.invoke with the four cases from its KDoc, in order. args is null for methods without parameters.
Write the class half of Interception.check: refuse a final class that has intercepted methods, then an intercepted method that is private or final, with the messages from the comment.

Run the tests. Most now fail with your own message: SettlementService is final, so no subclass can intercept it.... Open SettlementService and its two @Timed methods. Leave region() final. Run until all twelve pass.
hints: In Kotlin, Any::class.java is java.lang.Object. That is what method.declaringClass is for equals, hashCode and toString.
InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, *a) needs a non-null array: use args ?: emptyArray() once at the top.
If gives up after the last attempt sees UndeclaredThrowableException, your target call threw the InvocationTargetException itself. Throw e.cause!!.
If the self-call test logs only settle, audit is still final: open on the class doesn't open its members.
lab.done: All twelve tests in InterceptionTest pass, and region() is still final.

drill.title: The four-case handler from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write an InvocationHandler for a target and a Map<Method, List<Interceptor>> that answers Object methods by identity, runs default methods with invokeDefault, runs every other method through its chain, and unwraps InvocationTargetException. Then compare. Which case did you write last, and does the order matter?

answer.html: class InterceptingHandler( private val target: Any, private val chains: Map<Method, List<Interceptor>>, ) : InvocationHandler { override fun invoke(proxy: Any, method: Method, args: Array<Any?>?): Any? { val a = args ?: emptyArray() if (method.declaringClass == Any::class.java) return when (method.name) { // 1. identity "equals" -> proxy === a[0] "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy) else -> "Proxy[$target]" } if (method.isDefault) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, *a) // 2. this = proxy return Invocation("${method.declaringClass.simpleName}.${method.name}", a, chains[method].orEmpty()) { try { method.invoke(target, *a) } // 3. the chain, then the target catch (e: InvocationTargetException) { throw e.cause!! } // 4. unwrap }.proceed() } }

alt.html: final class InterceptingHandler implements InvocationHandler { private final Object target; private final Map<Method, List<Interceptor>> chains; InterceptingHandler(Object target, Map<Method, List<Interceptor>> chains) { this.target = target; this.chains = chains; } @Override public Object invoke(Object proxy, Method method, Object[] args) throws Throwable { Object[] a = args == null ? new Object[0] : args; if (method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) { // 1. identity return switch (method.getName()) { case "equals" -> proxy == a[0]; case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy); default -> "Proxy[" + target + "]"; }; } if (method.isDefault()) return InvocationHandler.invokeDefault(proxy, method, a); // 2. this = proxy String name = method.getDeclaringClass().getSimpleName() + "." + method.getName(); return new Invocation(name, a, chains.getOrDefault(method, List.of()), () -> { try { return method.invoke(target, a); } // 3. the chain, then the target catch (InvocationTargetException e) { throw sneaky(e.getCause()); } // 4. unwrap }).proceed(); } // Callable.call() may throw Exception but not Throwable: rethrow the cause unchanged @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") private static <E extends Throwable> E sneaky(Throwable t) throws E { throw (E) t; } }

recap: An interceptor runs around a call and calls proceed() to go on; a chain of them ends in the real method. Retry calls proceed() again. @Timed outside @Retry times what the caller waited for.

A component with interfaces gets a JDK proxy around a separate target. The handler answers equals, hashCode and toString by identity, runs default methods with invokeDefault, runs the chain, and unwraps InvocationTargetException.
A JDK proxy is not an instance of the class, and only sees the interface's methods: ask for the interface, and put the annotations there.

A component without interfaces gets a Byte Buddy subclass, built with its real constructor arguments. It is the bean, so self-calls are intercepted, but it can't extend a final class or override a final or private method.
Kotlin is final by default. Open the class and the intercepted methods, use all-open (or kotlin-spring), or add an interface, and let the container refuse at start-up what it can't intercept.
Retry only listed failures, rethrow the original, retry the inner calls of a default method, and only repeat calls that carry an idempotency key. Nested retries multiply.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why the container uses two kinds of proxy instead of always generating a subclass with Byte Buddy. Explain what each kind gives up, and how the container decides.
explain.answer: A JDK proxy needs only an interface. It works on final Kotlin classes and costs no bytecode library, but it is a separate object in front of the target: the bean isn't an instance of the class, the annotations must be on the interface, and self-calls inside the target skip the interceptors. A subclass is the bean itself, so self-calls are intercepted and the object is an instance of the class, but it can only intercept what it can override: no final classes, no final or private methods, which in Kotlin means writing open or using all-open. The container uses the JDK proxy whenever the component implements an interface, because that path has fewer ways to fail silently, and a subclass only when there is no interface. In both cases it checks at start-up and refuses what it can't intercept.

deeper.html:
Jakarta Interceptors, the spec behind CDI and Quarkus, has the same pieces under other names. An interceptor binding is an annotation like @Timed that is itself annotated @InterceptorBinding. The interceptor is a class with an @AroundInvoke method that takes an InvocationContext and calls ctx.proceed(). The order of the chain comes from @Priority on each interceptor class, with lower numbers running first. Spring AOP's equivalent is an AOP Alliance MethodInterceptor, whose invoke(MethodInvocation) also ends in proceed(), ordered by @Order or the Ordered interface.

Annotations and proxies have a quieter interaction too. Java annotations are not inherited from interfaces: @Timed on CardIssuerClient.authorize is not visible through FakeIssuer.class.getMethod("authorize", ...). A JDK proxy hands the handler the interface's Method, so the lab's container sees it. A subclass proxy looks at the class's methods, so an annotation that lives only on an interface method would not be found there. Spring papers over this with its own annotation search, which walks interfaces and superclasses. The lab refuses the ambiguous case instead: annotations on the class of an interface-proxied component are an error.

Byte Buddy can also load a generated class without a new class loader. ClassLoadingStrategy.UsingLookup with a MethodHandles.Lookup from the bean's package defines the subclass in the same loader and package as its superclass, which lets it override package-private methods and avoids one loader per class. The default used in the lab is the simplest one, and lesson 3's histogram shows what it leaves behind.
